results.verified_title: China and Limits to the European Union's Geoeconomic Turn
results.source_identity_basis: The Wiley JCMS full-article page carries the exact assigned DOI 10.1111/jcms.70140 and title; body sections on 5G and export controls were readable, and the assigned 2026-07-06 date is consistent with its 2026 provenance.
results.evidence_location: Article comparative case discussion of 5G and export-control competences
results.specific_finding: Two independently readable 2026 studies establish a structural governance constraint in EU–China technological and research relations: national discretion in Dutch semiconductor export licensing coexists with EU-level research-security eligibility and screening measures; China-directed knowledge/equipment flows are governed across both EU and member-state levels.
results.primary_evidence_summary: The JCMS study analyzes EU geoeconomic power toward China by comparing 5G risk governance and export controls, showing persistent member-state authority. An independently published July 2026 open-access study of EU–China research cooperation (2021–2025) maps EU-level research-security rules and continued but increasingly screened cooperation, giving a distinct source and complementary mechanism.
results.corroboration_assessment: Independent Springer paper (different authors and domain) documents EU de-risking restrictions and continued research cooperation; Dutch government’s licensing change independently confirms member-state authority. Together they validate structural governance fragmentation but cannot prove effects on Chinese R&D productivity.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: EU research-security rules plus country-level licensing/spectrum controls create fragmented project eligibility, information-flow and high-end-equipment pathways facing China-linked scientists and firms.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Exact main-Radar topic. confirms: Because export controls and 5G security remain member state competences, they are hard tests of EU geoeconomic power, and the EU frames China primarily as a source of direct risks rather than a broad strategic rival. — Main-Radar description is supported as an interpretation of EU institutional competences, but not verified as a China technology-performance finding.
results.method_and_limitations: Both papers are policy-document/comparative analyses, not quantitative measurements of Chinese technology capability. Dutch controls evidence policy action, not effects on Chinese patenting, deployment or bilateral grant flows. The valid finding is an institutional constraint, not China technological weakness.
results.reviewer_notes: PROMOTED on recheck: second fully open independent scholarly analysis separately substantiates the China-linked research-security pathway. Keep country attribution limited to EU–China links, not China-owned capacity.

results.verified_title: When R&D workforce expansion does not translate into innovation capability: evidence from Türkiye’s Technopark ecosystem
results.source_identity_basis: Opened full article text hosted via Oxford Academic institutional gateway: author Erşan Ciğerim, journal Science and Public Policy, DOI 10.1093/scipol/scag087, first published 31 October 2026. The underlying canonical OUP URL redirects unsuccessfully in this environment, but its DOI, title and body match in gateway page.
results.evidence_location: Full article sections 3.1–3.3 (sampling/analysis), 4 (R&D FTE time series), 6.1–6.4 (interview themes) and 7.2 (limitations).
results.specific_finding: A 2026 Marmara-region qualitative study (38 manager/engineer interviews across eight technoparks and two R&D centres, as stated in its methods) identifies four practical constraints on conversion of rapidly expanding R&D employment into innovation: project competence, digital skills, mid-career retention, and unequal knowledge exchange.
results.primary_evidence_summary: Opened the full 2026 Science and Public Policy article, including methods, cited interview excerpts, Tables 1–4, policy context and limitations. TurkStat/Eurostat 2024 FTE R&D personnel 310,473; the EU Commission’s 4 Nov 2026 Türkiye report independently confirms approximately 310,473 FTE personnel and 1.46% R&D/GDP for 2024, plus innovation performance of 57% of EU average in EIS 2026.
results.corroboration_assessment: European Commission Türkiye 2026 country report independently reports workforce scale and limited innovation relative to EU; secondary Eurostat-based time series confirms 2007–2024 workforce growth. Neither independently replicates interviews or establishes headcount causing an output gap.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Personnel headcount growth requires complementary organisational absorptive capacity: mentoring, practical project work, AI/data-skills training, experienced researcher retention and firm–university knowledge-transfer routines.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Not identified in supplied main Radar. not in main radar: Abstract Many emerging economies use science, technology and innovation policy to expand R&D personnel, but larger research workforces do not necessarily generate stronger innovation capability. This article examines this problem through Türkiye as an illustrative emerging-economy case, where R&D personnel and researcher numbers have grown rapidly while selected innovation-output indicators continue to signal unresolved capability gaps. Drawing on comparative secondary indicators and semi-struct — Search metadata supports study design, not yet all substantive results; do not turn a single qualitative study into an economy-wide measured trend.
results.method_and_limitations: Purposeful, nonrandom Marmara sample of better-performing technoparks; observations cannot be projected to every Turkish firm or interpreted causally. Important internal arithmetic inconsistency: Table 1 states 18 managers and 20 engineers (total 38) but manager row counts listed as 14+4+4=22, alongside engineer 17+3=20. Verify table with author before quantitative use. 2024 FTE researcher figure is explicitly an estimate, not directly in official bulletin.
results.reviewer_notes: PROMOTED after obtaining full original article and independent EU Commission/Eurostat comparison. Table 1 participant subtotals do not reconcile; do not cite disputed subgroup numbers or claim national representativeness.

results.verified_title: Rethinking dual-use in quantum technology
results.source_identity_basis: Full open-access Springer EPJ Quantum Technology editorial, exact DOI 10.1140/epjqt/s40507-026-00560-5, by Michal Krelina and Ulrich Mans, published 26 August 2026; sections 1–4 opened.
results.evidence_location: Abstract and sections 2–4 (US/UK foundational funding, European reception, dual-use governance)
results.specific_finding: 2026 review of ten quantum dual-use studies documents a long-standing US/UK defence–science integration, contrasting the historically civilian-only EU research framework. In 2026 the US set out integrated quantum economic- and national-security R&D programmes.
results.primary_evidence_summary: Krelina and Mans, EPJ Quantum Technology editorial 13:91 (26 Aug 2026), introduction and sections 2–4, trace predominantly US/UK defence-funded quantum origins and the later EU debate; note the 2026 EU framework shift toward selected dual-use funding.
results.corroboration_assessment: Two separate US government agencies document June/July 2026 integrated economic-security quantum policy and operational R&D aims, corroborating the institutional structure described by the academic authors; both are policy claims rather than independently audited success measures.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Early defence/intelligence R&D, a coordinated National Quantum Initiative, and connected sensing/computing/networks pathways help quantum technology transfer across civilian and security applications. The source chiefly describes governance/institutions, not defence deployments.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Exact main-Radar topic. extends: The authors argue quantum technology has been dual-use since its foundational experiments, that this origin story is predominantly Anglo-American, and that dual-use denotes a status rather than resolving normative questions. — Extends US/EU contrast with concrete 2026 programmes; avoid presenting dual-use potential as validated battlefield impact.
results.method_and_limitations: Editorial/synthesis of ten themed contributions, not causal evaluation or a newly demonstrated machine. White House executive order and NSF Project Triad are statements of US policy and launch, not independent proof that deployment succeeded.
results.reviewer_notes: Extends US/EU contrast with concrete 2026 programmes; avoid presenting dual-use potential as validated battlefield impact.

results.verified_title: Cleantech innovation, industrial decarbonisation and global competition: Focus on China
results.source_identity_basis: Opened European Parliament Directorate-General for Economy, Transformation and Industry publication record and substantive executive synopsis: Focus on China briefing, Johanna Krebs, DOI 10.2861/2519824, released 17 September 2026. The downloadable PDF was not separately read.
results.evidence_location: EU publication record: full substantive policy synopsis (industrial support, market protection, R&D/industrial clusters) and IEA Energy Technology Perspectives 2026 chapter supply-chain capacity statistics
results.specific_finding: A 2026 European Parliament briefing identifies China’s long-lived industrial policy model—demand subsidies, producer support, temporary localisation and integrated industrial clusters—as a mechanism for clean-technology scaling. Independently, IEA finds China has around 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply-chain production capacity (2024), supporting a structural industrial-strength finding, not the causal contribution of each policy.
results.primary_evidence_summary: Opened and read the publisher’s substantive synopsis and matched author, report DOI and September 2026 date. The briefing explains coordinated capacity targets, temporary localisation rules, supplier/customer incentives and risk absorption. The IEA 2026 supply-chain section independently reports Chinese concentration in solar and batteries.
results.corroboration_assessment: Independent international energy agency tracks supply-chain concentration and 2020–2025 investment history; supports China structural scale, not a proven causality chain from individual subsidies or a 2026 production milestone.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Policy-backed early industrial scaling, dense upstream/downstream clusters, manufacturing learning cycles and large R&D pools create low-cost manufacturing and rapid iteration. EU implications are supply-chain dependency, industrial diversification and R&D-to-scale coordination.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Exact main-Radar topic. confirms: China’s long-term industrial policy and clustered value chains generate system-wide competitive pressure on European cleantech industries and research/innovation investment. — Not promoted to verified findings.
results.method_and_limitations: Full 2026 policy briefing PDF was not independently opened; only its substantive issuing-body synopsis was visible. IEA production-capacity shares differ by technology and base year; market share/production capacity is not innovation efficiency or quality. Industrial policy causality remains qualitative.
results.reviewer_notes: PROMOTED with independent IEA manufacturing-capacity measures; narrow to independently supported structural difference, not complete causal proof of subsidy effects.

results.verified_title: WIPO Global Innovation Index 2026 — cross-country innovation benchmarking
results.source_identity_basis: WIPO GII 2026 Russia country profile publicly indexed and read with country rank, time series, rank confidence interval and 2024–2025 venture-deal change, tied to 2026 GII public release dated 29 September 2026.
results.evidence_location: WIPO country profile: GII Ranking (2020–2026), Innovation Inputs/Outputs, Global Innovation Tracker short-term measures; independent Dsight Venture Eurasia 2025 industry survey summary
results.specific_finding: Russia’s WIPO GII ranking moved from 45th in 2021 to 58th of 139 in 2026 (rank uncertainty 52–65), while its 2026 tracker finds a sharp 2024–2025 decline in venture deal counts. A separate Dsight 2025 venture dataset also reports a large decline in deal counts (42%) and investment (10%) for its own Russian market sample.
results.primary_evidence_summary: Opened/read WIPO 2026 ranking and time-series snippets: inputs rank 71, outputs rank 55, Russian VC deal count change -59.7% for its tracked 2024–25 series. 2026 rank is 58 vs 2025 rank 60; the longer 2021–26 period shows deterioration but most recent year modestly improves.
results.corroboration_assessment: Independent market trackers separately report declining Russian VC volume/deal count; figures differ from WIPO because populations, definitions and samples differ. Do not state the WIPO -59.7% was replicated.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Shrinking venture deal volumes constrain commercialization and startup scale-up despite continued scientific and industrial activity; Russia’s input/output rankings and longer run trajectory suggest an imbalanced innovation-system environment.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Not identified in supplied main Radar. not in main radar: Cross-country benchmarking, check country coverage and availability of Russia; missing data cannot support a finding. — Preserve as benchmark lead; do not treat a composite rank improvement as evidence of recovered innovation performance.
results.method_and_limitations: GII composite rankings are sensitive to indicator set, publication lags and measurement uncertainty (2026 rank confidence band 52–65). VC data coverage uncertain and possibly sparse under sanctions; rank is not an evaluation of defence R&D or proof of economic-policy causation.
results.reviewer_notes: PROMOTED: WIPO multi-year Russia profile triangulated by separate Dsight 2025 VC market study; estimates must not be merged.

However, existing industrial policy frameworks remain insufficient to capture the complexity and dynamics of contemporary industrial systems and policies. To address this gap, this study proposes a novel industrial policy analysis framework comprising four analytically distinct yet interrelated dimensions: drivers shaping policy, value-chain segme — New not-in-main-Radar structural finding on Japan’s policy mix; coded interventions are study-defined, not observed productivity.

results.verified_title: Statistical Communiqué on National Expenditures on Science and Technology in 2025
results.source_identity_basis: Opened exact official communiqué issued by China NBS/MOST/MOF, signed 16 October 2026, posted 17 October. Final 2025 statistics supersede February 2026 preliminary estimates.
results.source_type: official China R&D expenditure statistical survey
results.evidence_location: Final national 2025 R&D communiqué sections on performer type, basic vs applied vs experimental R&D and GDP intensity; independently compiled NSF international 2024 spending comparison plus WIPO 2026 China global innovation output indicators
results.specific_finding: China’s official finalized 2025 R&D survey reports CNY 3,928.82bn spending (+8.2% nominal YoY), 2.80% GDP intensity, CNY 283.46bn basic research, and 77.4% enterprise-performed expenditure; the broader scale/intensity shift is directionally consistent with independently compiled earlier-year NSF international R&D indicators and WIPO 2026 measures of Chinese research and patenting output, but precise 2025 Chinese figures remain official estimates.
results.primary_evidence_summary: Final official R&D survey details verified against February preliminary estimates: original 3,926.2bn/8.1% were revised to 3,928.82bn/8.2%. Reviewed NSF international 2024 indicators and WIPO 2026 China profile as separate-method evidence of research scale and outputs rather than as external audit of 2025 financial totals.
results.corroboration_assessment: NCSES 2026 international comparison and WIPO 2026 innovation indicators independently place China among major global R&D and output systems and support a multi-year scale/intensity structural difference. Neither re-measures China’s CNY 3,928.82bn 2025 outlay or validates the 77.4% enterprise share.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: High enterprise R&D share, increasing research-intensity and basic-research funding enlarge national capacity for industrial and scientific programmes; the path from spending to productivity or social returns requires independent outcome evaluation.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Not identified in supplied main Radar. not in main radar: Chinese 2025 R&D expenditure release, including basic-research share and intensity. Government-reported statistics are primary evidence of reported figures; compare with OECD methodology and independent series. — Differentiate source date (Oct 16), posting (Oct 17) and package record (Oct 19).
results.method_and_limitations: Statistical survey not audited by an independent external body for 2025 totals; growth nominal unless adjusted. Cross-country PPP/currency, denominator and reporting convention changes complicate comparison. VERIFY official number as an official report, NOT externally audited actual GDP-normalized innovation output.
results.reviewer_notes: PROMOTED as independently directionally corroborated multi-year structural R&D-intensity trend; exact 2025 CNY amounts explicitly described as self-reported, not external-validation claims. Candidate #15 dropped as duplicate preliminary release.

results.verified_title: WIPO Global Innovation Index 2026 — China innovation and global clusters
results.source_identity_basis: Official WIPO GII 2026 China country PDF opened and first-page screenshot inspected, showing 2026 rank 10, input/output breakdown; WIPO master 2026 index cross-checked.

results.specific_finding: WIPO ranks China 10th in Global Innovation Index 2026 (among 139 countries), with notably stronger innovation output than input components (output rank 5, input rank 22) and 25 of the world’s top 100 science/technology clusters.

results.verified_title: Semiconductors in EU–Taiwan Relations: Bridging Gaps, Building Trust

results.specific_finding: A 2026 Institut Montaigne policy report finds EU–Taiwan semiconductor cooperation is substantial but asymmetric: Taiwanese manufacturing know-how and supply-chain control complement European equipment/materials capacity, while regulation/security complicate closer links.
results.primary_evidence_summary: Mathieu Duchâtel, Semiconductors in EU–Taiwan Relations: Bridging Gaps, Building Trust (28 Apr 2026), original PDF report, summary and policy sections opened; report draws on ~40 expert interviews.
results.corroboration_assessment: European Commission State aid announcement independently confirms the Taiwanese-European ESMC joint venture, German public-aid authorization and future factory timetable; government approval is not evidence of completed fabrication.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Investment-backed joint fabrication and expertise transfer (including TSMC/Bosch/Infineon/NXP ESMC project in Dresden) can embed Taiwanese foundry methods into Europe’s chips ecosystem; political and trade restrictions affect collaboration.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Exact main-Radar topic. extends: The paper identifies gaps in EU-Taiwan semiconductor relations and argues for trust-building measures as the basis for deeper cooperation. — Avoid claiming 2026 operational output at ESMC Dresden: investment and State aid are planned/project-stage.

results.reviewer_notes: Avoid claiming 2026 operational output at ESMC Dresden: investment and State aid are planned/project-stage.

results.verified_title: The Neo-Academic Cold War: Political Traumas and Transnational Paranoia
results.source_identity_basis: Full open Springer High Education Policy essay by John Aubrey Douglass, DOI 10.1057/s41307-026-00465-z, dated 10 Aug 2026, includes China-specific discussion of altered collaboration networks; author-affiliation is not assumed to set China geography.
results.evidence_location: Full essay sections on Chinese/global transnational science cooperation, cited bibliometrics, new semi-autonomous networks; independent OECD STI Outlook 2025, scientific cooperation chapter Figures 2.1–2.4; US NSF NCSES 2026 collaboration article
results.specific_finding: The essay’s structural claim of fragmentation in science cooperation is corroborated in narrower observable terms: OECD analysis of Scopus finds China’s international collaboration intensity declined over 2020–2023 mainly through fewer US–China co-authored papers while China–EU research links continued to strengthen; NSF reports China international coauthor share was 16% in 2024, down from a 2018 peak of 22%.
results.primary_evidence_summary: Full 2026 policy essay discusses China as one of several emerging international research networks and gives cross-country context, but its geopolitical framing is interpretive. Independent OECD 2025 bibliometrics and US NCSES 2026 reveal China-specific collaboration trends, supporting a structural China cooperation finding instead of claims of universal global isolation.
results.corroboration_assessment: Separate OECD/NSF sources based on Scopus/Science-Metrix bibliometrics validate directional international-coauthor decline and continuing links; they do not prove the essay’s causal political claims, nor support blanket assertion that China–EU cooperation fell.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Restrictions, security screening, geopolitical risk and domestic coauthor capacity can shift scientific knowledge flows; China’s international cooperation is rebalanced rather than uniformly shut down.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Exact main-Radar topic. confirms: Global science is fragmenting into semi-autonomous cooperation silos under multipolar rivalry, with China and Europe positioned as relative beneficiaries of US decline and open science and collective problem-solving as the principal casualties. — Do not infer China is the sole actor or assume author affiliation determines geography of an academic-cold-war claim.
results.method_and_limitations: The essay is interpretive and polemical; strong assertions about political intent should not be represented as measured science. Independent bibliometrics pertain to 2018–2024 not full 2026, differ by database and counting methods, and cannot isolate policy causality.
results.reviewer_notes: PROMOTED only after narrowing claim to internationally cross-checked China coauthorship trend; avoid presenting author opinion as fact or extrapolating global four-silo scheme from data.

results.verified_title: Shared gains, secure links: rethinking EU-Asia digital cooperation – CEPS
results.source_identity_basis: CEPS original PDF with matching title Shared gains, secure links: rethinking EU–Asia digital cooperation, named researchers and June 2026 report identity; summary-page screenshot inspected.
results.evidence_location: CEPS report executive summary, country-partnership modes and digital cooperation recommendations
results.specific_finding: A June 2026 CEPS analysis identifies an EU–Asia digital cooperation architecture in which Taiwan participates mainly through practical sectoral, research, industry and member-state routes rather than an EU–Taiwan formal Digital Partnership; legal/geopolitical constraints shape access.
results.primary_evidence_summary: CEPS report Shared gains, secure links by Ergenc and co-authors, June 2026, original PDF summary, stakeholder/partnership discussion and recommendations read and cover screenshot checked. EU bilateral science-cooperation records document existing Taiwan collaboration mechanisms.
results.corroboration_assessment: European Commission lists Taiwan-related R&I co-funding arrangements; independent Institut Montaigne policy study describes concrete EU–Taiwan semiconductor collaboration; corroborates informal and practical links, not the lack of formal Digital Partnership by itself.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Project-level science funding, digital standards dialogue and supply-chain research ties allow cooperation with Asian partners under different political and legal structures; Taiwan’s route differs from formally established EU digital partnerships.
results.eu_radar_comparison: Exact main-Radar topic. extends: EU-Asia digital partnerships operate in a fragmented ecosystem without unifying institutional or legal architecture, so goals remain underachieved; the authors recommend anchoring alignment in research and innovation collaboration, broadening engagement beyond governments, and using sectoral minilateral formats, with non-recognition-dependent channels for Taiwan. — Distinguish an EU Digital Partnership treaty-type label from existing EC/Taiwan co-funding and bilateral science arrangements.
results.method_and_limitations: Policy-options synthesis and interviews, not causal outcome evaluation; avoid claiming that Taiwan has zero formal EU research links or that no cooperation mechanism currently exists. The EC lists existing co-funding arrangements.
results.reviewer_notes: Distinguish an EU Digital Partnership treaty-type label from existing EC/Taiwan co-funding and bilateral science arrangements.
